01.note: A man was alone in a house with a married woman. When the owner of the house came in, the man burst through the wall of palm branches and ran away. Rava ruled that the woman remains permitted to her husband: had the man actually sinned, he would have hidden inside rather than expose himself by fleeing in the open.
01.why: The Gemara is collecting cases about when suspicion of adultery forbids a wife to her husband. After two cases where Rav Nahman dismissed a wife's own claims, here Rava reasons from the man's behavior that nothing happened.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the woman stays permitted to her husband.

terms.meaning: A married woman who committed adultery becomes forbidden to her husband. Saying she is permitted means the marriage continues as before.

02.note: Two cases are told. In the first, a man alone in a house with a married woman burst through the palm-branch wall and fled when the owner came in. In the second, an adulterer hid behind the door when a woman's husband came home; seeing that a snake had tasted some cress lying there, he warned the husband not to eat it. In both, Rava ruled the wife permitted to her husband: the first man would have hidden had he sinned, and the second, had he sinned, would have preferred that the husband eat and die, for the verse links adultery with blood on the hands.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting cases about when suspicion of adultery forbids a wife to her husband. It then asks what Rava's cress ruling adds, and answers that one might have thought the adulterer saved the husband only to keep enjoying the forbidden wife.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled in both cases that the wife remains permitted to her husband.

terms.meaning: A married woman who committed adultery becomes forbidden to her husband. Saying she is permitted means the marriage continues as before.
A leafy plant eaten as a vegetable. A snake tasting it was feared to leave venom in it.

02.flag: The STORY span joins two separate incidents (the palm-wall escape and the cress), each told as its own case.

03.note: Shimon HaTzaddik, a priest, said he had never eaten the guilt-offering of a nazirite who had become impure, except once. A handsome young man from the South came to him with beautiful eyes and curled locks. Shimon asked why he would destroy such hair. The man said that while shepherding for his father he saw his reflection in a spring, his evil inclination rose up against him, and he swore to shave his hair for the sake of Heaven. Shimon rose, kissed him on the head, and said: may there be more nazirites like you in Israel.
03.why: The Gemara asked why Rabbi Shimon does not learn from the words "to the Lord" that one can vow to be a nazirite like Samson. The answer: those words are needed to teach that a nazirite vow should be made purely for the sake of Heaven, as this young man's was.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A priest who tells of the one impure nazirite whose offering he ate.

people.name: the man from the South
people.about: A young shepherd who became a nazirite to subdue his pride in his looks.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
An offering a nazirite must bring after becoming ritually impure, after which he starts his term again. Shimon avoided eating it because such nazirites often regretted their vows.
In rabbinic thought, the inner urge that pushes a person toward sin or arrogance.

04.note: Queen Helene vowed that if her son came home safely from war she would be a nazirite for seven years. He returned and she kept the vow. Then she went up to the Land of Israel, where Beit Hillel told her to observe seven more years. At the end of those she became impure and had to begin again, so she was a nazirite for twenty-one years. Rabbi Yehuda said it was only fourteen.
04.why: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda's "fourteen" assumes. It reasons that if he followed Beit Shammai's thirty extra days he would have said fourteen years and thirty days, so he must follow Beit Hillel and hold she never became impure.

people.name: Queen Helene
people.about: A queen who made a nazirite vow for her son's safe return from war.

people.name: Beit Hillel
people.about: The school of Hillel, who told her to observe seven more years in the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who said her naziriteship lasted only fourteen years.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
Two early schools of Sages, followers of Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on points of law.
Ritual impurity, here from contact with the dead, cancels the days a nazirite has counted and forces a new start.

04.flag: The STORY segments are the Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's view; the narrative of Queen Helene itself is in the mishna in segment 1 and is only quoted in part here.

05.note: Rabbi Hanina's father vowed that his young son would be a nazirite, and they brought the boy before Rabban Gamliel, who examined him to see whether he had reached physical maturity (Rabbi Yosei says: whether he had reached the age of vows). The boy said: My teacher, do not trouble to examine me. If I am a minor, I will be a nazirite because of my father; if I am an adult, I will be one because of my own vow. Rabban Gamliel rose, kissed him on the head, and said he was certain this boy would become an authority of law for Israel. Within a few years the boy was issuing rulings.
05.why: Two Sages disagree about how long a father can impose a nazirite vow on his son: until physical maturity, or until the age of vows. The Gemara asks whether that dispute matches the two versions of what Rabban Gamliel was checking for in this story.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: As a boy, his father vowed he would be a nazirite; he later issued rulings for Israel.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who examined the boy and predicted his greatness.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who gives a different account of what Rabban Gamliel was checking.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
The appearance of two pubic hairs, the legal sign of physical maturity.
The age, about a year before adulthood, at which a child's own vows begin to count if he understands them.

06.note: Rabbi Yitzhak was a priest whose father died in Ginzak, and he was told only three years later. He went to ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Elisha and four Elders with him whether he could make himself impure to handle his father's remains. They answered that the verse "for his father" allows a priest to become impure only when the body is whole, not when it is lacking, as it would be after three years. The text does not say what he then did.
06.why: Rav had ruled that a priest may not become impure for a relative whose body is incomplete, and a baraita seemed to contradict him. The Gemara answers that Rav follows the Sages of this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A priest who learned of his father's death three years late.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Elisha
people.about: A Sage who, with four Elders, answered Rabbi Yitzhak's question.

terms.meaning: A priest (kohen) must not become ritually impure through contact with the dead, except to bury close relatives such as a father.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

07.note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students in, calling them vexatious people who came only to overwhelm him with legal points. Sumakhos, one of them, forced his way in and quoted Rabbi Meir's teaching that a nazirite shaves for impurity from a corpse and from an olive-bulk of a corpse. Rabbi Yehuda grew angry: if an olive-bulk requires shaving, all the more so a whole corpse, so why list it? Rabbi Yosei said: people will say Meir is dead, Yehuda is angry and Yosei kept silent, and what will become of the Torah? He answered that the teaching is needed for a corpse that does not have an olive-bulk of flesh.
07.why: The mishna's list of impurities for which a nazirite shaves begins with "a corpse", which seems unnecessary. This story raises that problem, and the Gemara goes on to offer further answers from Rabbi Yohanan and Rava.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose death opens the story; his students were barred.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who barred Rabbi Meir's students and grew angry at Sumakhos.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: A student of Rabbi Meir who forced his way into the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who spoke up so the question would not go unanswered.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
The size of an olive, the smallest amount of a corpse that imparts impurity.
A nazirite who becomes impure from the dead shaves his head and starts his term again.

08.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that there were six things Rabbi Akiva had declared impure and the Sages pure, and that Rabbi Akiva retracted. In one incident, people brought a box full of bones to the synagogue of the blacksmiths and set it down in the open air. Todos the doctor and all the doctors with him came in, examined it, and said: there is not a spine from one corpse here. The incident itself does not state the ruling that followed.
08.why: The Gemara is asking whether the mishna's "a spine and skull" means both together or either one alone. It tries to prove from the doctors' finding that either one is enough, then rejects the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabbi Akiva's six rulings and this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who had ruled six things impure and later retracted.

people.name: Todos the doctor
people.about: A physician who, with other doctors, examined the box of bones.

terms.meaning: A collection of early teachings that parallels and adds to the Mishna.
The box was kept out from under the roof, because human remains under a roof make everything beneath it impure.

09.note: Rabbi Eliezer tells of going to a place called Ardaskeya, where he found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Petter Rosh teaching before Rabbi Meir: impurity from a corpse that makes a nazirite shave also makes one liable for entering the Temple, and impurity that does not, does not. Rabbi Meir objected that such impurity should be no more lenient than that of a creeping animal. Rabbi Eliezer asked Rabbi Meir whether he knew Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel; Rabbi Meir said yes, and Rabbi Eliezer told him that Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel had taught him this very rule in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua.
09.why: The mishna gives this rule as Rabbi Eliezer's in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, though the story shows he learned it through Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel. From this the Sages learn that in a chain of three, the middle name is dropped.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who tells the story and traces his source for the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Petter Rosh
people.about: A Sage found teaching the rule before Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who objected to the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel
people.about: The Sage from whom Rabbi Eliezer had learned the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The original source of the rule, as quoted by Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
A person who is ritually impure is forbidden to enter the Temple and is liable for doing so.
Certain small creatures, such as rodents and lizards, whose dead bodies make a person ritually impure.

10.note: Rav Huna ruled that an adult who rounds a boy's head is liable to lashes. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked him: then who shaves your sons? Rav Huna answered: Hova, my wife. Rav Adda bar Ahava said: Hova should bury her sons. The Gemara reports that for all the years Rav Adda bar Ahava was alive, Rav Huna's children did not survive.
10.why: Shmuel explained that the mishna's shaving case involves a woman or a boy, who are not bound by the ban on rounding the head. Rav Huna's ruling adds that an adult man who shaves a boy is still liable, and the Gemara then traces both Sages' views to the verse.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who ruled that a man who rounds a boy's head is liable.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who disputed Rav Huna's ruling and cursed his wife.

people.name: Hova
people.about: Rav Huna's wife, who shaved their sons.

terms.meaning: Shaving the hair at the sides of the head, which the Torah forbids men to do (Leviticus 19:27).
Flogging, the court's punishment for breaking certain Torah prohibitions.

11.note: A man was found liable to lashes before Rabbi Ami. When his clothes were removed for the flogging, his armpit was exposed, and Rabbi Ami saw that he had not shaved it. Rabbi Ami told his attendants: Leave him; this is one of those who are meticulous in keeping the commandments.
11.why: The Gemara has been discussing whether a man may shave his armpit hair, which Rabbi Yohanan forbids. Rabbi Ami treats leaving it unshaved as a sign of a man who keeps the commandments carefully.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who sat in judgment and released the man.

terms.meaning: Flogging, the court's punishment for breaking certain Torah prohibitions.
People known for careful observance, including rules that ordinary people do not keep.

12.note: Rabbi Yeshevav searched an area and found two corpses that were already known and one found for the first time, and he wanted to declare the place a graveyard. Rabbi Akiva told him: all your toil was in vain. A graveyard is declared only for three known corpses or three found for the first time.
12.why: The discussion sets out when finding bodies turns a place into a graveyard, and a baraita has just ruled that known and newly found corpses do not combine. This incident shows Rabbi Akiva applying that rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yeshevav
people.about: A Sage who wanted to declare a site a graveyard.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who told him his effort was wasted.

terms.meaning: When three corpses are found buried in the usual way, the site is treated as a burial ground, which affects whether the bodies may be moved and how the area is treated for purity.

terms.term: known and found for the first time
terms.meaning: "Known" corpses were already known to be buried there; the others were discovered for the first time.

13.note: The Roman government sent word to its garrison at Beth Peor: show us where Moses is buried. When the men stood on the upper part of the mountain, the grave seemed to be below; when they stood below, it seemed to be above. They split into two groups, and still those above saw it below and those below saw it above. So the verse was fulfilled: "no man knows of his grave to this day."
13.why: Rabbi Berekhya has just pointed out that the Torah describes Moses' burial place very precisely and yet says no one knows it. This story shows that even with the location in hand, the grave could not be found.

terms.meaning: A place in the land of Moab; the Torah says Moses was buried in the valley opposite it.
A post of soldiers stationed in a place.

14.note: Rabbi Meir recalled that while studying with Rabbi Akiva he put iron sulfate in the ink, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing. When he came to Rabbi Yishmael, he was asked his work and said he was a scribe. Rabbi Yishmael warned him that adding or leaving out one letter could destroy the whole world. Rabbi Meir replied that he put iron sulfate in his ink. Rabbi Yishmael asked: may that be put in ink? The Torah says of the sota scroll "he shall blot them out", so the writing must be erasable. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir meant he did not even fear a fly rubbing out part of a letter. A second version reverses the order of his teachers and which one forbade it; the Gemara explains he studied with Rabbi Akiva, then Rabbi Yishmael, then Rabbi Akiva again.
14.why: The mishna describes the sota ritual, in which curses written on a scroll are blotted out into the water she drinks. This story establishes that such writing must be erasable, and the Gemara goes on to say which sacred writings may use iron sulfate.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe and student who added iron sulfate to his ink.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A teacher who warned Rabbi Meir about his work as a scribe.

terms.meaning: A substance added to ink that makes writing hard to erase.
A wife suspected of adultery who undergoes a Temple ritual: curses are written on a scroll, blotted into water, and she drinks it.
Two Hebrew letters that differ only by a small corner; rubbing it off turns one into the other.

14.flag: STORY segments 6-10 continue past the exchange into the Gemara's analysis and its resolution of a contradiction between two versions of the account.

15.note: Rav Dimi reported that Hillel and Shevna were brothers. Hillel devoted himself to Torah study and stayed poor, while Shevna went into business and grew rich. In the end Shevna said to Hillel: come, let us join together and divide, offering half his wealth for half the reward of Hillel's study. A Divine Voice went out and said: "If a man would give all the fortune of his house for love, he would utterly be condemned."
15.why: Ulla explains that this verse is not about people like those who supported a scholar from the start; it is about someone like Shevna, who tried to buy a share of Torah study after the fact.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A brother who devoted himself to Torah and remained poor.

people.name: Shevna
people.about: Hillel's brother, a wealthy businessman who offered to trade wealth for a share in his merit.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: The Sage who brought this report to Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing a message or a ruling.

16.note: There was a widow who had a synagogue in her own neighborhood, yet every day she came to pray in Rabbi Yohanan's study hall. Rabbi Yohanan said to her: My daughter, is there not a synagogue near you? She answered: My teacher, do I not get a reward for the steps?
16.why: A teaching lists a widow who keeps visiting neighbors among those who erode the world. The Gemara challenges this with Rabbi Yohanan's saying that he learned about earning reward from a widow; this is that widow.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage in whose study hall the widow prayed.

people.name: the widow
people.about: A woman who walked past her local synagogue to pray farther away.

terms.meaning: A house of Torah study, where prayers were also held.
The idea that each step taken on the way to a commandment, such as prayer, earns its own reward.

17.note: Before his death, King Yannai told his wife: do not fear the Pharisees, nor those who are not Pharisees, but the hypocrites who look like Pharisees, whose deeds are like those of Zimri and who ask for a reward like that of Pinehas.
17.why: The Gemara is going through a list of kinds of false, showy piety. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak has just said that the heavenly court will punish those who wear the cloak of the righteous, and Yannai's warning makes the same point.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: A king who gave this warning to his wife.

terms.meaning: The group that followed the Sages' teaching; the king contrasts them with those who are not Pharisees.
In Numbers 25, Zimri sinned openly with a Midianite woman and Pinehas killed him, earning God's reward.

18.note: Yohanan the High Priest heard a Divine Voice coming from the Holy of Holies, saying: the youths who went to wage war in Antokhya have been victorious. Another time, Shimon HaTzaddik heard a Divine Voice from the Holy of Holies saying: the decree the enemy meant to bring against the Temple is annulled, Gaskalgas has been killed and his decrees voided. People wrote down the time, and it matched. The voice spoke in Aramaic.
18.why: Rabbi Yohanan had said the ministering angels do not understand Aramaic, so prayers should not be said in it. The Gemara challenges him with these Aramaic voices and answers that a Divine Voice is different, or that it was Gabriel, who knows every language.

people.name: Yohanan the High Priest
people.about: A high priest who heard a voice announcing a victory.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A sage who heard a voice announcing the enemy's death.

people.name: Gaskalgas
people.about: An enemy of the Temple (identified as Caligula) whose death was announced.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing a message.
The innermost room of the Temple, entered only by the High Priest.
The everyday language of many Jews in that era, close to Hebrew but distinct from it.

19.note: Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to the same place. Rabbi Abbahu taught stories and lore, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba taught law. Everyone left Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and went to Rabbi Abbahu, and Rabbi Hiyya was offended. Rabbi Abbahu told him a parable: when one man sells precious stones and another sells small trinkets, the crowd rushes to the one with trinkets. Every day Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba used to escort Rabbi Abbahu to his lodging out of respect for the emperor's house; that day Rabbi Abbahu escorted Rabbi Hiyya to his lodging instead, and even so Rabbi Hiyya's mind was not at ease with him.
19.why: Rabbi Abbahu has just said he once thought himself humble, and the Gemara asks what his humility was. This is one of several examples it gives.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage linked to the emperor's house, whose talks drew the crowd.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who taught law and was offended when his audience left.

terms.meaning: The non-legal parts of rabbinic teaching: stories, sayings and interpretations of verses.
Jewish law, and the study of its rules.

20.note: At the public Torah reading of the Sukkot festival, the king usually received the Torah scroll standing and read it sitting. King Agrippa stood, received it and read standing, and the Sages praised him. When he reached the verse "You may not appoint a foreigner over you", tears flowed from his eyes, because he came from the house of Herod and was not of Jewish origin, and the whole people told him: you are our brother. A teaching in the name of Rabbi Natan says that at that moment the Jewish people were sentenced to destruction for flattering Agrippa. Along the way the Gemara asks how a king could sit in the Temple courtyard, answering that it was the women's courtyard, and why the Sages praised a king for giving up his honor, answering that a commandment is different.
20.why: The Gemara is working through the mishna's account of the king's Torah reading at the Sukkot assembly. Rabbi Natan's comment then leads the discussion to the damage done by flattery.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king of Herod's house who read the Torah standing at the assembly.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who taught that flattering Agrippa brought a sentence of destruction.

terms.meaning: An outer courtyard of the Temple, where sitting was permitted.
A polite phrase meaning the Jewish people themselves, used to avoid saying something harsh about them directly.

20.flag: The STORY segments interleave the mishna's account of Agrippa with the Gemara's legal questions on it.
